summary: BIER forwards multicast without per-flow state in the core. The ingress router decides which egress routers need a packet and puts that information in a header. This document defines the BIER encapsulation for MPLS and non-MPLS networks.

plainLanguage.summary: BIER forwards multicast traffic without building a tree or keeping state per flow. The trick is in the packet header: it carries a row of bits, one per router in the network, and the bits that are set say which routers should get a copy. This document defines that header, byte for byte.

subtitle: The exact header that lets a multicast packet carry a bit for every router that should receive it.

tldr.problem: BIER forwards multicast without per-flow state, but routers need to agree on one header format that carries the set of egress routers, in both MPLS and non-MPLS networks.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress router wraps each packet in a BIER header whose BitString has one bit per egress router. In MPLS the first four octets double as the bottom MPLS label stack entry; in non-MPLS networks a domain-wide BIFT-id takes the label's place.
tldr.outcome: The encapsulation lets every router read the BitString, find the right forwarding table and replicate the packet as needed. It has no cryptographic protection, so BIER packets should not be accepted from untrusted interfaces.

today: RFC 8296 is listed as a Proposed Standard published in January 2018, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The document itself states that it is not an Internet Standards Track specification and that it defines an Experimental Protocol, published for examination, experimental implementation and evaluation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The BIER architecture describes a new approach to the forwarding of multicast data packets. Known as 'Bit Index Explicit Replication', it provides optimal forwarding of multicast data packets through a multicast domain, without requiring any explicit tree-building protocol and without requiring intermediate nodes to maintain any per-flow state.

A router that supports BIER is known as a Bit-Forwarding Router. A BIER domain is a connected set of such routers, each of which has been assigned a BFR-prefix, a routable IP address used to identify it. A packet enters a BIER domain at a Bit-Forwarding Ingress Router and leaves at one or more Bit-Forwarding Egress Routers. Each router of a given BIER domain is provisioned to be in one or more sub-domains, and in the context of a given sub-domain each ingress and egress router must have a BFR-id that is unique within that sub-domain. A BFR-id is a number in the range [1,65535] that identifies a router uniquely within a sub-domain.

BIER requires that multicast data packets be encapsulated with a header that provides the information needed to support the BIER forwarding procedures. That information includes the sub-domain to which the packet has been assigned, a Set Identifier, a BitString, and a BitStringLength. Together these values identify the set of egress routers to which the packet must be delivered.

This document defines an encapsulation that can be used in either MPLS networks or non-MPLS networks, but the construction and processing of the BIER header are slightly different in the two. The handling of certain fields is different depending on whether the underlying network is an MPLS network, and in an MPLS network the first four octets of a BIER header are also the bottom entry of an MPLS label stack.

Following the BIER header is the payload, which may be an IPv4 packet, an IPv6 packet, an Ethernet frame, an MPLS packet, or an Operations, Administration and Maintenance packet. The BIER header contains a Next Protocol field identifying the type of the payload. If the payload is an MPLS packet, an MPLS label stack immediately follows the BIER header, and the top label of that stack may be either a downstream-assigned or an upstream-assigned label.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router in a BIER network gets a number that is unique inside its sub-domain. A packet's header carries a row of bits, one per router, and the routers whose bits are set are the ones that must receive a copy.

sections.title: The BIER Header
sections.content:
The BIER header begins with the BIFT-id, which represents a particular Bit Index Forwarding Table. Each such table corresponds to a particular combination of sub-domain, BitStringLength and Set Identifier. The default BitStringLength value for the encapsulations defined in the document is 256.

In an MPLS network the first four octets of the header carry the Traffic Class field, the S bit and the TTL field, as in any other MPLS label stack entry. The remaining fields follow. The Nibble field is set to the binary value 0101 in an MPLS network, which ensures that the MPLS equal-cost multipath logic will not confuse the remainder of the BIER header with an IP header or with the header of a pseudowire packet; a BFR that receives a BIER packet with any other value in the first nibble after the label stack SHOULD discard the packet and log an error. In a non-MPLS network the Nibble field SHOULD be set to 0000 upon transmission but MUST be ignored upon reception.

The Ver field is a 4-bit field identifying the version of the BIER header, and the document specifies version 0. If a packet is received by a BFR that does not support the specified version, the BFR MUST discard the packet and log an error. The value 0xF is reserved for experimental use and MUST NOT be assigned by any future IETF document or by IANA.

The BSL field is a 4-bit field encoding the length in bits of the BitString. When parsing the BIER header, a BFR MUST infer the length of the BitString from the BIFT-id and MUST NOT infer it from this field, which is present only to enable offline tools such as LAN analysers to parse the header. Only certain values are supported: 1 for 64 bits, 2 for 128 bits, 3 for 256 bits, 4 for 512 bits, 5 for 1024 bits, 6 for 2048 bits and 7 for 4096 bits. A received packet with any other value SHOULD be discarded and an error logged.

The Entropy field is a 20-bit field specifying a value that can be used for load-balancing purposes. The BIER forwarding process may do equal-cost load balancing, in which case the procedure MUST choose the same path for any two packets that have the same entropy value and the same BitString.

The OAM bits are set to 0 by the ingress router by default and are not modified by other routers; they have no effect on the path taken or on the quality of service applied. The Rsv bits are currently unused, SHOULD be set to 0 upon transmission and MUST be ignored upon reception. The DSCP field is not used by default in MPLS networks, and all six bits SHOULD be set to 0 upon transmission and ignored upon reception; in non-MPLS networks it MAY hold a Differentiated Services Codepoint.

The Proto field is a 6-bit Next Protocol field identifying the type of the payload, populated from the 'BIER Next Protocol Identifiers' registry. If an egress router receives a BIER packet but does not recognise or support the value, it SHOULD discard the packet and log an error. The BFIR-id field is, by default, the BFR-id of the ingress router in the sub-domain to which the packet has been assigned, encoded as an unsigned integer in the range [1,65535].

The BitString holds the bits that, together with the packet's Set Identifier and sub-domain, identify the destination egress routers. The Set Identifier and sub-domain are not carried explicitly in the BIER header, because a particular BIFT-id always corresponds to a particular Set Identifier and sub-domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The header has a fixed layout: which forwarding table to use, how long the packet may live, what the payload is, and the row of bits naming the destination routers.

sections.title: Encapsulation in MPLS Networks
sections.content:
When a BIER domain is both an IGP domain and an MPLS network, each router is assumed to use IGP extensions to advertise a set of BIER-MPLS labels. When the domain contains a single sub-domain, a router needs to advertise one label for each combination of Set Identifier and BitStringLength; if the domain contains multiple sub-domains, it needs one label per Set Identifier per BitStringLength for each sub-domain. In some environments the only routing protocol in a BIER domain might be BGP, in which case BGP extensions can be used to advertise the necessary labels.

The BIER-MPLS labels are locally significant, that is, unique only to the router that advertises them, downstream-assigned MPLS labels. Penultimate hop popping MUST NOT be applied to a BIER-MPLS label. The label corresponding to a particular combination of sub-domain, Set Identifier and BitStringLength is interpreted as representing the forwarding table that corresponds to that same combination, so the label performs the function of a BIFT-id, and this label value is carried in the BIFT-id field of the encapsulation.

It is crucial that in an MPLS network the first four octets of the BIER encapsulation header are also the last four octets of the MPLS header, so any prior MPLS label stack entries MUST have the S bit clear. The S bit of the BIER-MPLS label itself MUST be set to 1. The TTL field is the usual MPLS Time to Live field, and when a BIER packet is forwarded to one or more router adjacencies, the BIER-MPLS label carried by the forwarded packet MUST have a TTL field whose value is one less than that of the packet's incoming TTL.

If a BIER packet's incoming TTL is 1 or greater and one of the bits in its BitString identifies the current router, then that router is an egress router for the packet and MUST process it as one, removing the BIER encapsulation and processing the payload based on the contents of the Proto field. If the incoming TTL is 0 the packet is considered expired, and if the incoming TTL is 1 and the BitString has a bit set that does not identify the current router the packet is also considered expired. Expired packets SHOULD be passed to an error-handling procedure, and optional implementation-specific rate limiting may be applied.

Note that if a received BIER packet has an incoming TTL of 1 and its BitString has a bit set identifying the current router, the payload MUST be processed by that router, but the packet MUST NOT be forwarded further, and it SHOULD also be passed to the error-handling procedures for expired packets.
sections.plainLanguage: In an MPLS network the first four bytes of the BIER header double as an ordinary MPLS label, so the packet travels like any other labelled packet until a router recognises its own label.

sections.title: Encapsulation in Non-MPLS Networks
sections.content:
In non-MPLS networks, a BIFT-id MUST be assigned for every combination of sub-domain, Set Identifier and BitStringLength that is to be used in that network. The correspondence between a BIFT-id and a particular triple is unique throughout the BIER domain and is known to all the routers in it. The means by which the BIFT-ids are assigned and made known are outside the scope of the document. In an MPLS network the BIFT-id is an MPLS label, so its value may change as a BIER packet goes from router to router; in a non-MPLS network, since the BIFT-id is domain-wide unique, it is not expected to change as a BIER packet travels.

By default the Traffic Class field has no significance in a non-MPLS network, and should be set to the binary value 000 upon transmission and ignored upon reception. The S bit has no significance either; it should be set to 1 upon transmission and ignored upon reception. The TTL field is the BIER Time to Live field, whose purpose is to prevent BIER packets from looping indefinitely in the event of improper operation of the control plane.

A BIER packet may itself need to be carried inside another encapsulation, for example an Ethernet frame or a UDP packet, in which case the BIER packet is the payload of the outer encapsulation. The document assumes that the frame or packet carrying a BIER packet as its payload is a unicast frame or packet: although a BIER packet is a multicast packet, the frame carrying it is unicast from one router to the next.

In an MPLS network the outer encapsulation's next protocol codepoint for MPLS MUST be used, and if the outer encapsulation has a codepoint for MPLS with a downstream-assigned label and a different one for MPLS with an upstream-assigned label, the codepoint for MPLS with a downstream-assigned label MUST be used. For example, if a BIER packet is encapsulated in an Ethernet frame, the Ethertype MUST be 0x8847.

In a non-MPLS network the outer encapsulation's next protocol codepoint MUST be set to a value that means 'non-MPLS BIER', and a codepoint that means MPLS, with either upstream-assigned or downstream-assigned labels, MUST NOT be used. By requiring a distinct codepoint, non-MPLS BIER can coexist with non-BIER MPLS, and the BIFT-id values used by the former will not conflict with MPLS label values used by the latter. Therefore, if a non-MPLS BIER packet is encapsulated in an Ethernet header, the Ethertype MUST NOT be 0x8847 or 0x8848. IEEE has assigned Ethertype 0xAB37 for non-MPLS BIER packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Outside MPLS there is no label to carry the table number, so a number that means the same thing everywhere in the network is used instead, and a separate Ethernet type marks the packet as BIER.

sections.title: Imposing and Processing the Encapsulation
sections.content:
Each ingress router is expected to know the Maximum Transmission Unit of the BIER domain and also the size of the BIER encapsulation, so it can deduce the maximum size of the payload that can be encapsulated in a BIER packet, a size the document calls the BIER-MTU. If an ingress router receives a multicast packet from outside the BIER domain and the packet size exceeds the BIER-MTU, it takes whatever action is appropriate for a multicast packet that is too large to be forwarded to all its next hops: if that is to drop the packet and advertise an MTU to the source, it drops the packet and advertises the BIER-MTU; if the appropriate action is to fragment the packet, the procedures below are applied to each fragment in sequence.

The ingress router then consults the multicast flow overlay to determine the value of the Proto field and the set of egress routers that must receive the packet. If more than one sub-domain is supported, it assigns the packet to a particular sub-domain. It looks up the BFR-id, in the given sub-domain, of each of the egress routers, and converts each such BFR-id into Set Identifier and BitString format.

All the BFR-ids that have the same Set Identifier can be encoded into the same BitString. For each distinct Set Identifier that occurs in the list of the packet's destination egress routers, the ingress router makes a copy of the multicast data packet and encapsulates the copy in a BIER header. The header contains the BitString representing all the destination egress routers whose BFR-ids, in the given sub-domain, correspond to the given Set Identifier, and it also contains the ingress router's own BFR-id in the sub-domain to which the packet has been assigned. The ingress router then applies the BIER forwarding procedure to that copy, which may result in one or more copies of the packet, possibly with a modified BitString, being transmitted to a neighbouring router.

If the non-MPLS BIER encapsulation is being used, the BIFT-id field is set to the BIFT-id that corresponds to the packet's sub-domain, Set Identifier and BitStringLength, and the TTL is set according to policy. If the MPLS BIER encapsulation is being used, the ingress router finds the BIER-MPLS label that the neighbour advertised as corresponding to the given combination, and prepends a label stack containing that one label, with the S bit set to indicate the end of the stack and the TTL set according to policy.

When an intermediate router processes a received MPLS packet and one of its own BIER-MPLS labels rises to the top of the label stack, the router infers the BitStringLength from the label, and the Set Identifier and sub-domain are implicitly identified by it as well. If it forwards a copy of the packet to a neighbouring router, it first swaps the label at the top of the stack with the BIER-MPLS label that the neighbour advertised for the same combination, and the TTL field of the outgoing BIER-MPLS label MUST be one less than the incoming TTL. When an intermediate router processes a received non-MPLS BIER packet, it infers the BitStringLength from the BIFT-id and the Set Identifier and sub-domain are likewise implicit, and it then follows the BIER forwarding procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: The ingress router works out which routers must receive the packet, turns their numbers into bits, and stamps the header. Each router along the way reads its own bit, forwards the packet on with the right label, and copies it where the bits say more copies are needed.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has set up a registry called 'BIER Next Protocol Identifiers', with a registration policy of IETF Review. The initial values are 0 for Reserved, 1 for an MPLS packet with a downstream-assigned label at the top of the stack, 2 for an MPLS packet with an upstream-assigned label at the top of the stack, 3 for an Ethernet frame, 4 for an IPv4 packet, 5 for an OAM packet, 6 for an IPv6 packet, and 63 for Reserved. IEEE has assigned Ethertype 0xAB37 for non-MPLS BIER packets.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the list of payload types that can follow the header, and IEEE has set aside an Ethernet type for the non-MPLS form.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Insofar as the document makes use of MPLS, it inherits any security considerations that apply to the use of the MPLS data plane. If a BIER encapsulation header is modified in ways other than those specified, packets may be lost, stolen or otherwise misdelivered. Such modifications are likely to go undetected, because the BIER encapsulation does not provide cryptographic integrity protection.

Layer 2 encryption can be used to ensure that a BIER-encapsulated packet is not altered while in transit between adjacent routers. If a router itself is compromised, there is no way to prevent the compromised router from sending incorrect packets. BIER-encapsulated packets should generally not be accepted from untrusted interfaces or tunnels: an operator may wish to have a policy of accepting them only from interfaces to trusted routers and not from customer-facing interfaces.

There may be applications that require a router to accept a BIER-encapsulated packet from an interface to a system that is not controlled by the network operator, for instance a virtual machine in a data centre that submits BIER-encapsulated packets to a router. In such a case it is desirable to verify that the packet is from a legitimate source and that its BitString denotes only systems to which that source is allowed to send. The BIER encapsulation itself provides no way to verify that the source is legitimate, that it really is the system denoted by the BFIR-id, or that it is allowed to set any particular set of bits in the BitString. Insofar as the document relies on IGP extensions, it inherits any security considerations that apply to the IGP, and the security considerations of the BIER architecture apply as well.
sections.plainLanguage: The header carries no protection of its own, so a change to it would go unnoticed. Encryption between neighbouring routers is the way to guard against that.

fields.name: BIFT-id
fields.desc: Identifies the forwarding table to use. In an MPLS network this field carries the BIER-MPLS label.

fields.name: TC
fields.desc: The usual MPLS Traffic Class field.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: The MPLS bottom-of-stack bit. It must be 1 for the BIER label and 0 for any label before it.

fields.name: TTL
fields.desc: The MPLS Time to Live field, used to stop BIER packets looping.

fields.name: Nibble
fields.desc: Set to 0101 in an MPLS network so that equal-cost multipath logic does not mistake the header for an IP or pseudowire header.

fields.name: Ver
fields.desc: The version of the BIER header. This document specifies version 0.

fields.name: BSL
fields.desc: The length in bits of the BitString. Parsers must infer the length from the BIFT-id instead.

fields.name: Entropy
fields.desc: A value for load-balancing. Packets with the same entropy and the same BitString take the same path.

fields.name: OAM
fields.desc: Set to 0 by default and not modified by other routers.

fields.name: Rsv
fields.desc: Currently unused. Should be set to 0 on transmission and ignored on reception.

fields.name: DSCP
fields.desc: Unused by default in MPLS networks; may hold a Differentiated Services Codepoint in non-MPLS networks.

fields.name: Proto
fields.desc: Identifies the type of the payload that follows the header.

fields.name: BFIR-id
fields.desc: The BFR-id of the ingress router, in the range [1,65535].

fields.name: BitString
fields.desc: One bit per egress router. A set bit means that router must receive the packet.

viz.caption: WHAT THE INGRESS ROUTER DOES (RFC 8296, SECTION 3)

items.title: Work out the destinations
items.text: Consult the multicast flow overlay for the payload type and for the set of egress routers that must receive the packet.

items.title: Choose a sub-domain
items.text: If more than one sub-domain is supported, the packet is assigned to one of them.

items.title: Turn numbers into bits
items.text: Look up the BFR-id of each destination router and convert each into Set Identifier and BitString form.

items.title: One copy per set identifier
items.text: For each distinct Set Identifier, a copy of the packet is made and wrapped in a BIER header carrying the matching BitString.

items.title: Label it for the next hop
items.text: In an MPLS network the BIER-MPLS label for that combination is pushed on the stack, with the S bit set and the TTL set by policy.
